extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funders, policy-makers and administrators concerned with research funding, peer review and evaluation of grant schemes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts criteria, policies and measurement approaches used to characterise and evaluate bias, burden, conservatism, innovation and creativity in research grant funding and peer review. Focuses on funder practices, assessment criteria, and metrics for portfolio evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application submission limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit applicants to a fixed number of submissions (e.g. NIH clause limiting applicants to two submissions of a research proposal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy aims to increase first-time applicant success and reduce average time-to-award; has been adopted by NIH and ERC. Reported effects: higher proportion of first-time applications awarded; reduction in average time to award (Rockey, 2012). Potential community pushback noted (Benezra, 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-stage application process with graded first stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a two-stage application where proposals receive a first-stage score/category (e.g. A, B, C) and only top categories proceed; lower categories impose waiting periods before reapplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ERC example: A → proceed; B → wait one year; C → wait two years before reapplying to ERC programs. Reported outcome: decreased number of applications sent for full evaluation and shorter time between submission and outcome notification. NIHR two-stage adoption produced similar reductions in review workload (INT01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple calls per year
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer multiple funding calls across the year rather than a single annual deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces reviewer burden by decreasing applicants per round and reduces applicant burden by allowing ongoing rolling application opportunities (INT01; Herbert et al., 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant application length limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the permitted length of grant applications (e.g. NIH reduced length from 25 to 12 pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objective: reduce administrative burden on applicants and reviewers and to focus on concept and impact rather than detailed methods. Guidance to applicants: focus away from routine methodological detail toward describing how the application is innovative. Evidence: shortening applications may slightly increase applicant preparation time (Barnett et al., 2015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding period length as a policy lever
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust the award duration (e.g. suggesting extending funding period to five years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer funding periods can reduce application burden (fewer reapplications) and provide more scope for exploration and innovation (Bolli, 2014).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition(s) of 'innovative research' used by funders
rubrics_metrics.description: Different organisations define innovation variably (e.g. NIH: research that challenges and seeks to shift current research or clinical practice paradigms through new theoretical concepts, approaches or methodologies; AHA: research that may introduce a new paradigm, challenge current paradigms, add new perspectives or exhibit uniquely creative qualities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions often emphasise high-risk/high-reward, novelty (new paradigms/approaches), and potential for improvements in patient care (clinical fields). Funders may operationalise definitions via expert judgement or formal criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure innovation via reviewer disagreement (controversy metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lack of agreement between reviewers (e.g. variance or negative kurtosis of scores) as a surrogate metric for innovation/controversy in proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kaplan (2007) suggests metrics such as variance or negative kurtosis to capture observations in the tails of grading distributions; new metrics proposed to quantify controversy between reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure innovation via productivity/output metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess innovation by tracking post-award outputs: production of high-impact journal articles, changes in investigators' research agendas, and the variety of journals citing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Azoulay et al. (2011) compared HHMI and NIH-funded investigators and found HHMI produced more high-impact articles and greater propensity to change. Liaw et al. (2017) suggest measuring changes in PI research agenda and breadth of citation impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure novelty via keyword/MeSH term analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify novelty through new combinations of keywords or MeSH terms in proposals relative to existing literature and a researcher's prior work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boudreau et al. (2016) used novel MeSH combinations to define highly novel proposals and found such proposals often scored lower when reviewers lacked relevant expertise; Liaw et al. (2017) also propose keyword novelty measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal assessment of innovation as an explicit review criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Include innovation as a scored criterion within the peer review assessment form (often allocated a percentage of the overall score).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example AHA questions: Does the project challenge existing paradigms and present an innovative hypothesis or address a critical barrier? Does the project develop or employ novel concepts, approaches, methodologies, tools or technologies for this area? Including innovation as criterion can incentivise applicants to include disruptive ideas (Guthrie et al., 2018).

rubrics_metrics.name: Out-of-order funding to support innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Select and fund some applications judged as innovative despite lower peer-review scores, i.e., fund 'out of order'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH practice: approximately 15% of funded applications selected out-of-order to prioritise innovation (Lindner & Nakamura, 2015). Intended to counter peer-review conservatism and support high-risk/high-reward work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce methodological detail requirement in applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly instruct applicants to limit routine methodological details and emphasise innovation in method descriptions (e.g. by shortening methods page allowance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NIH shortened methods section and provided guidance to focus away from routine details toward innovation (Lindner et al., 2016). This is intended to shift reviewer focus toward conceptual novelty rather than exhaustive methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate funding streams/schemes for innovative research
rubrics_metrics.description: Create dedicated schemes with different size/timeframe/selection rules targeted at high-risk/high-reward projects (e.g. New Innovator Award, Pioneer, Transformative R01, ZonMW 'off-road' program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such schemes often allocate smaller funds and shorter timeframes (e.g. ZonMW €100,000 for 1.5 years; NIHR tiers with £150,000 for 18 months). These schemes can encourage innovation but may require longer funding or different structures to nurture early-career innovators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote diversity and interdisciplinarity as levers for innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Advance underrepresented groups to leadership and promote interdisciplinary research to increase diversity-driven innovation and productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature suggests diversity (e.g. advancing women or underrepresented groups, interdisciplinary teams) positively impacts innovation (Magua et al., 2017; Bromham et al., 2016). Funders can design schemes or eligibility to promote these factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and mitigation of conservatism in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge peer review's inherent conservatism that provides incentives for incremental research and discourages radical/unexplored approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The literature characterises peer review as 'anti-innovation' (Azoulay et al., 2013; Fang & Casadevall, 2016; Guthrie et al., 2018). Strategies to mitigate include out-of-order funding, separate innovation streams, and reviewer/training changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and bibliometric approaches to measure fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quantitative analyses—statistical evaluation of funding data and bibliometrics—to detect and measure fairness/bias in funding allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 10 lists these approaches (statistical evaluation, bibliometrics, text mining, longitudinal analyses, experimental randomisation). These methods allow funders to assess systematic disparities across applicants/groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text mining and longitudinal analyses for fairness assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply text mining of proposals and longitudinal tracking of applications/awards to assess fairness, topic prioritisation, and evolution over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text mining can identify disciplinary or topical patterns; longitudinal designs help observe career and portfolio-level effects. Combined with bibliometrics, these provide a portfolio-level view of equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental randomisation to study bias and process effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use randomised or experimental assignment of proposals/reviewers to identify causal effects and reduce confounding when measuring bias and review outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Randomisation provides robust evidence (e.g. design used in Boudreau et al., 2016 where proposals and reviewers were randomised) and supports causal inference about reviewer-expertise interactions and novelty scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden measurement methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure application and review burden through surveys and time-tracking: post-submission applicant surveys, real-time recording of applicant time, and surveys of funders and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches capture where time and effort are expended and can quantify burden experienced by applicants, reviewers, funders and institutions (Table 10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorisation of bias dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise multiple axes of bias that may affect funding outcomes: applicant characteristics (gender, ethnicity), career stage, research field, institution, and reviewer characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature highlights at least five main areas where bias can emerge; measurement and mitigation strategies should consider each axis separately as well as their intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify loci of burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterise where burden is experienced within the funding system: applicants, reviewers, funding agency, and institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different policy levers affect different loci (e.g. multiple calls reduce applicant and reviewer peaks; application length reductions affect applicant preparation time and reviewer reading time). Measurement should disaggregate burden by locus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer-expertise mismatch effect on novel proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise that evaluators give lower scores to highly novel proposals when those proposals are outside the evaluator's field/expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence (Boudreau et al., 2016) shows novelty (e.g. new MeSH combinations) can be penalised by reviewers lacking relevant expertise; reviewers also tend to favour proposals in their own fields (Gerhardus et al., 2016). Assignment strategies or reviewer pools may be adapted to mitigate this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design choices across funding stages affect bias/burden/conservatism
rubrics_metrics.description: Map funding-scheme design features at different stages (priority-setting, call frequency, award size/length, granularity, targeted schemes) to likely impacts on bias, burden and conservatism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from Table 11: clear focus of calls may reduce disciplinary bias; annual calls may disadvantage those with caring responsibilities and increase burden; fewer larger awards may disadvantage early-career researchers; longer awards can permit exploration and reduce conservatism; availability of schemes for specific groups may address gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of surveys and qualitative intelligence to inform reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect stakeholder (applicant, reviewer, funder) qualitative and survey evidence to understand burden, incentives and operational consequences of policy changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-submission surveys, interviews and stakeholder feedback informed observed effects of policy changes (e.g. two-stage processes, multiple calls) in cited INT01–INT04 case studies. Combine with quantitative metrics for a fuller evaluation.
